center.name: Shaykh Ibrāhīm Niasse
center.bio: West African Muslim scholar, Sufi shaykh, and Quranic commentator. Born in Kaolack (Senegal), he became the foremost figure of the Fayḍah Tijāniyya movement. His tafsīr, delivered orally and transcribed from recordings, draws on the full range of Islamic scholarly tradition — hadith, tafsīr, kalam, and Sufi philosophy.

nodes.name: Al-Ghazālī
nodes.bio: Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī, theologian and Sufi philosopher. Author of Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn. Shaykh Ibrāhīm cites him in the body of the tafsīr — a primary intellectual interlocutor.

nodes.name: Al-Suyūṭī & Al-Maḥallī
nodes.bio: Jalāl al-Dīn al-Maḥallī (d. 864/1459) began, and his student Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī (d. 911/1505) completed, the joint Qurʾān commentary Tafsīr al-Jalālayn. Cited throughout — overwhelmingly via al-Ṣāwī's marginal commentary (Ḥāshiyat al-Ṣāwī ʿalā al-Jalālayn) — as a single unit, hence the combined entry.

nodes.name: Al-Qurṭubī
nodes.bio: Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Qurṭubī, Andalusian Mālikī scholar. His al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān is the most-cited tafsīr in the apparatus.

nodes.name: Al-Ṭabarī
nodes.bio: Muḥammad ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī, foundational figure of classical tafsīr. His Jāmiʿ al-Bayān is the earliest comprehensive Arabic tafsīr.

nodes.name: Ibn Kathīr
nodes.bio: Ismāʿīl ibn Kathīr, Syrian Shāfiʿī scholar. His Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm is among the most cited works in the apparatus.

nodes.name: Al-Bukhārī
nodes.bio: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Bukhārī, compiler of the Ṣaḥīḥ. The most-cited hadith collection in the apparatus.

nodes.name: Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj
nodes.bio: Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj al-Nīsābūrī, compiler of the Ṣaḥīḥ. Equal with Bukhārī as the most-cited hadith source.

nodes.name: Al-Tirmidhī
nodes.bio: Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī, compiler of the Jāmiʿ (Sunan al-Tirmidhī). Third most cited hadith collection.

nodes.name: Abū Dāwūd
nodes.bio: Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī, compiler of the Sunan. Among the six canonical hadith collections.

nodes.name: Ibn Mājah
nodes.bio: Ibn Mājah al-Qazwīnī, compiler of the Sunan. Sixth of the six canonical hadith collections.

nodes.name: Al-Nasāʾī
nodes.bio: Aḥmad ibn Shuʿayb al-Nasāʾī, compiler of the Sunan al-Kubrā. Among the six canonical hadith collections.

nodes.name: Al-Rāzī
nodes.bio: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, theologian and philosopher. His Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb represents post-Avicennan rational theology in tafsīr.

nodes.name: Ismāʿīl Ḥaqqī al-Bursawī
nodes.bio: Ismāʿīl Ḥaqqī al-Bursawī (1653–1725), Ottoman Jelvetī Sufi scholar and author of Rūḥ al-Bayān — the primary comparative tafsīr text alongside Shaykh Ibrāhīm's own, cited both in the body of the tafsīr and in the compiler's apparatus.

nodes.name: Al-Junayd
nodes.bio: Abū al-Qāsim al-Junayd, foundational Sufi master of Baghdad. Cited in the body text — his presence signals the Sufi intellectual lineage Shaykh Ibrāhīm inhabits.

nodes.name: Ibn ʿArabī
nodes.bio: Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī, Andalusian Sufi philosopher. Author of al-Futūḥāt al-Makkiyya. His presence in the body text signals Shaykh Ibrāhīm's engagement with speculative Sufism.

nodes.name: Ibn al-Fāriḍ
nodes.bio: ʿUmar ibn al-Fāriḍ, Egyptian Sufi poet. His appearance in the body text reflects the literary-mystical dimension of Shaykh Ibrāhīm's exegetical register.

nodes.name: Aḥmad al-Tijānī
nodes.bio: Founder of the Tijāniyya order. Shaykh Ibrāhīm cites him in the body of the tafsīr — situating the commentary firmly within Tijānī spiritual authority.

nodes.name: Sīdī ʿAlī Ḥarāzim
nodes.bio: Companion of Aḥmad al-Tijānī and compiler of Jawāhir al-Maʿānī. His citation signals Shaykh Ibrāhīm's rootedness in Tijānī textual tradition.

nodes.name: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal
nodes.bio: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, hadith master and eponym of the Ḥanbalī legal school; compiler of the Musnad.

nodes.name: Al-Ṭabarānī
nodes.bio: Sulaymān ibn Aḥmad al-Ṭabarānī, compiler of the three Muʿjams (al-Kabīr, al-Awsaṭ, al-Ṣaghīr), major hadith reference works.

nodes.name: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh
nodes.bio: Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh al-Iskandarī, Shādhilī Sufi master, author of the Ḥikam (Aphorisms).

nodes.name: Ibn Hishām
nodes.bio: Jamāl al-Dīn Ibn Hishām al-Anṣārī, Arabic grammarian, author of Mughnī al-Labīb and Qaṭr al-Nadā.

nodes.name: Ibn Saʿd
nodes.bio: Muḥammad Ibn Saʿd, author of Kitāb al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kabīr, a foundational biographical/historical compendium.

nodes.name: Al-Nīsābūrī
nodes.bio: Identity uncertain / possibly composite: cited once (Lesson 3) for a Qiṣaṣ al-Anbiyāʾ attributed here to “al-Nīsābūrī,” and once (Lesson 38) for a Sufi saying attributed to “Shaykh Abū Muḥammad al-Nīsābūrī.” The Lesson 3 citation names the book ‘ʿArāʾis al-Majālis,’ which is standardly identified as al-Thaʿlabī's work — yet a separate footnote (Lesson 27) cites ‘al-Nīsābūrī’ and ‘al-Thaʿlabī’ side by side as distinct authorities. Kept separate from al-Thaʿlabī and al-Ḥākim al-Naysābūrī pending further verification; flagged for review.

nodes.name: Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī
nodes.bio: Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, Egyptian Shāfiʿī ḥadīth master. Author of Fatḥ al-Bārī, the standard commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, cited repeatedly for hadith authentication and commentary.

nodes.name: Al-Ḥākim al-Naysābūrī
nodes.bio: Abū ʿAbdillāh Muḥammad ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Ḥākim al-Naysābūrī, compiler of al-Mustadrak ʿalā al-Ṣaḥīḥayn. Frequently cited for hadith authentication ("صححه الحاكم في مستدركه").

nodes.name: Al-Ṣāwī
nodes.bio: Aḥmad al-Ṣāwī, Egyptian Mālikī scholar. Author of Ḥāshiyat al-Ṣāwī ʿalā Tafsīr al-Jalālayn, a major marginal commentary heavily used throughout the apparatus.

nodes.name: Ibn ʿAbbās
nodes.bio: ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, cousin of the Prophet ﷺ and foundational figure of Qurʾānic exegesis; his interpretive reports (often via later transmitters) are cited constantly across the tafsīr.

nodes.name: Al-Shāfiʿī
nodes.bio: Muḥammad ibn Idrīs al-Shāfiʿī, eponym of the Shāfiʿī legal school. Cited for legal opinions and occasionally biographical anecdotes.

nodes.name: Al-Bayhaqī
nodes.bio: Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Bayhaqī, Shāfiʿī ḥadīth master. Author of Shuʿab al-Īmān and Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa, both cited as hadith sources.

nodes.name: Al-Khāzin
nodes.bio: ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn ʿAlī al-Khāzin, author of Lubāb al-Taʾwīl fī Maʿānī al-Tanzīl (Tafsīr al-Khāzin), cited as a tafsīr source.

nodes.name: Al-Nasafī
nodes.bio: ʿAbdullāh ibn Aḥmad al-Nasafī, author of Madārik al-Tanzīl wa-Ḥaqāʾiq al-Taʾwīl, cited as a tafsīr source (referenced here via his gloss/notes on al-Khāzin).

nodes.name: Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ
nodes.bio: ʿIyāḍ ibn Mūsā al-Yaḥṣubī, Mālikī judge of Ceuta. Author of al-Shifāʾ bi-Taʿrīf Ḥuqūq al-Muṣṭafā, the celebrated work on the Prophet's ﷺ merits, cited repeatedly.

nodes.name: Al-Ālūsī
nodes.bio: Maḥmūd al-Ālūsī, Baghdadi scholar and author of Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, a major late tafsīr cited especially in the later lessons.

nodes.name: Ibn Manẓūr
nodes.bio: Muḥammad ibn Mukarram Ibn Manẓūr, compiler of Lisān al-ʿArab, the major classical Arabic lexicon, cited for lexical explanations.

nodes.name: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
nodes.bio: ʿAbd al-Razzāq ibn Hammām al-Ṣanʿānī, early hadith compiler; author of al-Muṣannaf, cited for early narrations (often via his teacher Maʿmar).

nodes.name: Ibn Abī Shayba
nodes.bio: Abū Bakr ʿAbdullāh Ibn Abī Shayba, compiler of al-Muṣannaf, a major early hadith and narration collection cited in the apparatus.

nodes.name: Abū Ḥanīfa
nodes.bio: Nuʿmān ibn Thābit Abū Ḥanīfa, eponym of the Ḥanafī legal school, cited for legal opinions and biographical anecdote.

nodes.name: Al-Daylamī
nodes.bio: Shīrawayh al-Daylamī, compiler of al-Firdaws bi-Maʾthūr al-Khiṭāb, a hadith collection cited for narrations (dates uncertain for the exact compiler referenced).

nodes.name: Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī
nodes.bio: Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī, compiler of one of the earliest Musnad collections. Distinct from Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī (compiler of the Sunan), also cited in this tafsīr.

nodes.name: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī
nodes.bio: Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, early Successor (tābiʿī), renowned ascetic and exegetical authority, frequently quoted for moral and interpretive dicta.

nodes.name: Al-Bayḍāwī
nodes.bio: Nāṣir al-Dīn al-Bayḍāwī, author of Anwār al-Tanzīl wa-Asrār al-Taʾwīl, a widely used classical tafsīr.

nodes.name: Al-Nawawī
nodes.bio: Yaḥyā ibn Sharaf al-Nawawī, Shāfiʿī scholar. Author of al-Arbaʿūn al-Nawawiyya and the commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, cited for hadith commentary.

nodes.name: Ibn Qutayba
nodes.bio: ʿAbdullāh ibn Muslim Ibn Qutayba, author of al-Maʿārif and Gharīb al-Ḥadīth, cited for lexical and historical explanation.

nodes.name: Sībawayh
nodes.bio: ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān Sībawayh, foundational figure of Arabic grammar, author of al-Kitāb.

nodes.name: Al-Shaʿrānī
nodes.bio: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Shaʿrānī, Egyptian Sufi scholar, author of al-Anwār al-Qudsiyya, cited for Sufi anecdote and verse.

nodes.name: Al-Qushayrī
nodes.bio: ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Qushayrī, author of al-Risāla al-Qushayriyya, a foundational Sufi manual; cited here for an exegetical report.

nodes.name: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
nodes.bio: Athīr al-Dīn Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī, Andalusian grammarian and exegete, author of al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, cited for tafsīr and grammatical opinion.

nodes.name: Al-Dāraquṭnī
nodes.bio: ʿAlī ibn ʿUmar al-Dāraquṭnī, hadith critic, compiler of the Sunan al-Dāraquṭnī, cited for hadith transmission and criticism.

nodes.name: Ibn Ḥibbān
nodes.bio: Muḥammad Ibn Ḥibbān al-Bustī, compiler of Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān, cited as a hadith source.

nodes.name: Al-Ḥallāj
nodes.bio: Al-Ḥusayn ibn Manṣūr al-Ḥallāj, early and controversial Sufi figure executed in Baghdad; referenced here in a narrative/anecdotal context rather than as a cited textual authority.

nodes.name: Sahl al-Tustarī
nodes.bio: Sahl ibn ʿAbdillāh al-Tustarī, early Sufi exegete, among the earliest authors of a mystical Qurʾān commentary.

nodes.name: Al-Farrāʾ
nodes.bio: Yaḥyā ibn Ziyād al-Farrāʾ, Kūfan grammarian, author of Maʿānī al-Qurʾān, cited for lexical/grammatical explanation.

nodes.name: Ibn al-Jawzī
nodes.bio: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Ibn al-Jawzī, prolific Ḥanbalī scholar and exegete, cited for tafsīr opinion.

nodes.name: Al-Wāḥidī
nodes.bio: ʿAlī ibn Aḥmad al-Wāḥidī, author of Asbāb al-Nuzūl, cited for occasions of revelation and exegetical opinion.

nodes.name: Al-Thaʿlabī
nodes.bio: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Thaʿlabī, author of al-Kashf wa'l-Bayān and ʿArāʾis al-Majālis (Qiṣaṣ al-Anbiyāʾ), cited for tafsīr and prophetic narratives.

nodes.name: Al-Ashʿarī
nodes.bio: Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, eponymous founder of Ashʿarī theology (kalām). Cited once in the body text regarding the theological debate over whether the Prophet ﷺ saw God with his physical eyes during the Isrāʾ (Sūrat al-Najm).
